newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Angola says ready to extend control to UNITA areas.
newsitem.headline: Angola says ready to extend control to UNITA areas.

text.p: The Angolan government said on Monday it would begin extending its administration over territory controlled by the former rebel movement UNITA, but sceptics said they would believe it when they saw it happen.

"We will begin the programme of state administration tomorrow and it will be finished by the end of November," Minister of Territorial Administration Fernando Faustino Muteka told reporters in Luanda.
UNITA, the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola, fought a two-decade civil war against the government that ended with a peace treaty in 1994.
The United Nations has since overseen a precarious peace process that has recently threatened to unravel, say diplomats and officials close to the process.
Though the former rebels entered into a power-sharing agreement with the government in April, UNITA continues to control as much as 70 percent of the Angolan countryside.

UNITA's continued foot-dragging on handing over the land and its reluctance to define the number of men it still has under arms has brought a threat of imminent sanctions on the movement from the U.N. Security Council.

A plan for handing UNITA territory back to the government was suspended by UNITA in June after the movement's top representative to the peace process was beaten up by a crowd during a ceremony handing over a UNITA town.
Muteka said seven municipalities would be taken over by the government in four different interior provinces on Tuesday.

He also announced that the strategically important UNITA-held city of Negage in Uige Province and the city of Cuango, in a diamond-rich area of Lunda Norte, would be turned over to the government on Aug 29.

The decision was made at a meeting chaired by the Angolan government but attended by UNITA representatives, officials from the United Nations and the three observer nations to the peace process -- the United States, Portugal and Russia.
An official in the meeting reported that UNITA representative Isaias Samakuva apparently agreed to the plan.
"Samakuva said, 'Our leaders are predisposed to cooperate with this exercise. We support it'," said the official.
He said that although the plan looked like a big step in the peace process, it was no breakthrough.
"This is basically getting us back to where we were in June," said the official. "This will only be a breakthrough if these areas are actually turned over.

"They are talking about getting UNITA to give up all its territory, including Andulo and Bailundo, by the end of November, I don't see it happening," he said, referring to two key UNITA-held cities in the central highlands.
